paragraphs: Diffusion models generate outputs through a sequence of denoising steps, each requiring a neural network evaluation. Their sampling process can be understood as approximately solving a differential equation at selected noise levels. Those selected levels form the sampling schedule. This paper investigates how choosing that schedule more carefully can improve generation, alongside work on the numerical solver itself.

Align Your Steps uses methods from stochastic calculus to optimize schedules for particular combinations of solver, trained diffusion model, and dataset. The approach treats the placement of sampling steps as an optimization problem rather than relying on a manually designed rule. This matters because a limited number of network evaluations must be allocated across the denoising process.

The authors evaluate the approach on image generation, video generation, and two-dimensional toy data with several samplers. Optimized schedules outperform handcrafted alternatives in almost all reported experiments. The findings support schedule optimization as a useful component of diffusion sampling, especially when generation must use only a few steps.
icml-2024-align-your-steps-optimizing-sa.tldr: Align Your Steps optimizes diffusion sampling schedules and improves output quality over handcrafted schedules in almost all reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when several agents share a common objective but can access only local information and communicate through a network. The objective may be nonconvex and nonsmooth, so the target is a suitably defined approximate stationary point rather than a guaranteed global optimum. The central question is how many samples are needed to reach that target.

The proposed algorithm, Multi Epoch Decentralized Online Learning, connects online learning to nonconvex optimization. Its analysis first recovers the optimal convergence rate for smooth objectives. To handle nonsmooth objectives, the authors use randomized smoothing and Goldstein subdifferentials, mathematical tools for describing approximate stationarity when ordinary gradients are insufficient.

For the nonsmooth case, the authors establish sample complexity O(δ⁻¹ε⁻³), matching the optimal centralized counterpart in its dependence on these accuracy parameters. The first-order result does not require weak convexity. They also prove the same rate with a zero-order oracle, which supplies function values, without variance reduction. These are finite-time guarantees for approximate stationarity, not claims of finding the best possible objective value.
icml-2024-an-online-optimization-perspec.tldr: ME-DOL provides finite-time guarantees for decentralized nonsmooth nonconvex optimization using either first-order or zero-order information.

paragraphs: Finding a relevant document becomes difficult when the document is long and relevance depends on information spread across its text. Dividing it into smaller pieces may fail to preserve what makes it relevant. This paper addresses the linked problems of evaluating such retrieval, representing short queries alongside long documents, and training within GPU memory limits.

The authors introduce LoCoV1, a benchmark with 12 tasks where splitting documents into chunks is impossible or ineffective. They also build M2-BERT, an 80-million-parameter retrieval encoder based on the Monarch Mixer architecture. This state-space model handles documents of up to 32,000 tokens. A pretraining mixture supports both short and long sequences, while the retrieval fine-tuning method works with batches containing just one sample.

On LoCoV1, the encoder exceeds the competitive Transformer-based models by at least 22.2 points while using 90 times fewer parameters. The result ties the benchmark and training design together: the paper demonstrates strong retrieval performance specifically where understanding a long document as a whole matters.
icml-2024-benchmarking-and-building-long.tldr: LoCoV1 evaluates retrieval across long documents, and M2-BERT delivers strong results with a compact encoder and single-sample training batches.

paragraphs: Removing a component from a language model does not necessarily reveal its contribution in isolation: later components may change their behavior to compensate. This phenomenon is called self-repair. Earlier evidence came from narrow input distributions. The authors extend the investigation by ablating individual attention heads across multiple model families and sizes on the full training distribution.

They find that compensation occurs, but it is neither complete nor consistent. The removed head’s original direct effect is not fully restored, and the amount of repair varies substantially between prompts. Some prompts even produce overcorrection. This makes self-repair relevant to interpreting ablation experiments, because the observed outcome includes both the removed contribution and downstream responses to its removal.

The paper identifies two contributing mechanisms: changes in final LayerNorm scaling and sparse groups of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. It also discusses evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis, which predicts self-repair. That broader explanation is presented speculatively, distinct from the demonstrated compensation patterns and mechanisms.
icml-2024-explorations-of-self-repair-in.tldr: Language models partly compensate for removed attention heads, but the repair is prompt-dependent, imperfect, and sometimes excessive.

paragraphs: Strong performance on many tasks can coexist with failures involving accuracy, social bias, or alignment with human values. Understanding where these failures occur matters for debugging and auditing a model before deployment. The difficulty is that testing every possible combination of contributing factors is infeasible, leaving a need for methods that actively search for problematic behavior.

The authors introduce a method applied after model training that uses deep reinforcement learning to explore failure modes. Its aim is to construct a picture of where pretrained models go wrong, covering both discriminative models and generative models. This connects failure discovery to a search process rather than requiring exhaustive enumeration of possible test conditions.

The method then uses limited human feedback to shift behavior away from discovered failures, making the resulting failure landscape more desirable. Experiments across vision, language, and combined vision-language tasks demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines characterization and mitigation: discovering failure patterns supplies targets for subsequent improvement, without implying that every possible failure has been found or eliminated.
icml-2024-failures-are-fated-but-can-be-.tldr: A reinforcement-learning method searches pretrained models for failures and uses limited human feedback to reduce discovered unwanted behaviors.

paragraphs: BEAST is a gradient-free adversarial attack that uses beam search to find inputs that provoke unwanted language-model behavior. Its parameters expose tradeoffs among search speed, attack success, and prompt readability. The paper uses this computational efficiency to study several failure types: bypassing alignment, inducing incorrect answers, and improving privacy attacks.

In one reported comparison, BEAST jailbreaks Vicuna-7B-v1.5 in under a minute with 89% success on a single Nvidia RTX A6000 48GB GPU. A gradient-based baseline takes over an hour and reaches 70%. The authors also report adversarial suffixes that transfer to previously unseen prompts and models, including GPT-4-Turbo. These results demonstrate transfer in the investigated cases rather than a guarantee for every target.

Human evaluations find that an untargeted attack causes roughly 15% more incorrect Vicuna outputs than the unattacked condition, with irrelevant outputs occurring 22% of the time. BEAST also produces prompts within seconds that improve existing membership inference attacks. Together, the findings show how faster attack search can support investigation of multiple security and privacy weaknesses.
icml-2024-fast-adversarial-attacks-on-la.tldr: BEAST uses fast gradient-free search to expose jailbreak, hallucination, and privacy weaknesses in language models.

paragraphs: A model can use sensitive information that is difficult for a human observer to recognize in its inputs. The paper motivates this concern with prior findings that neural networks can infer racial information from X-ray scans. Such hidden information creates a risk that automated decisions depend on attributes the person using the model does not realize are present.

Existing orthogonalization and normalization approaches address unwanted information using foundations drawn from linear models. The authors extend these approaches with corrections for nonlinear operations such as ReLU activations. Their formulation supports both scalar predictions and tensor-valued outputs, allowing it to fit into neural network architectures with different output structures.

Experiments examine protection of sensitive information in generalized linear models, normalization of convolutional networks with respect to metadata, and correction of existing embeddings for unwanted attributes. The reported effectiveness supports adapting these correction methods to nonlinear models. The practical contribution is a broader mechanism for addressing specified unwanted information, rather than treating linear-model corrections as automatically adequate inside nonlinear architectures.
icml-2024-generalizing-orthogonalization.tldr: The paper extends orthogonalization methods to nonlinear models and demonstrates corrections for sensitive information, metadata, and unwanted embedding attributes.

paragraphs: Attention is expensive partly because data must move between a small, fast memory where computation occurs and a larger, slower memory. This paper studies that movement directly. It asks whether FlashAttention already minimizes the number of slow-memory accesses, and whether the answer changes with the amount of available fast memory.

Using N for the attention-matrix dimension, d for the head dimension, and M for cache size, FlashAttention requires N²d²/M input/output operations. The authors prove a matching lower bound, up to constant factors, when M is at least d². This result also covers algorithms using fast matrix multiplication, so changing to that computational technique cannot improve the bound in this regime.

When M is smaller than d², the paper gives an algorithm with lower input/output complexity and proves optimality within the class of combinatorial algorithms. The analysis connects communication complexity to memory-access complexity through a matrix-compression protocol. The outcome is a memory-regime-dependent answer about data movement, rather than an unrestricted claim that FlashAttention is optimal in every computational sense.
icml-2024-i-o-complexity-of-attention-or.tldr: FlashAttention is I/O-optimal up to constants when M ≥ d², while smaller caches admit an improved algorithm.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks can be trained by measuring how well their predictions satisfy an equation. When that equation contains integrals, constructing even one training residual may require a very large number of network evaluations. Approximating the integral seems natural, but the authors show that an unbiased integral estimate can still produce a biased training loss and a biased solution.

The paper investigates three ways to address this problem: deterministic sampling, a double-sampling trick, and a delayed target method. The key distinction is between accurately estimating an integral on average and correctly optimizing the loss built from that estimate. The proposed approaches address the consequences of approximation for learning, not just the cost of evaluating the equation.

Tests cover Poisson problems with singular charges and weak solutions in up to ten dimensions, electromagnetic problems involving a Maxwell equation, and Smoluchowski coagulation. Numerical results confirm that the bias occurs in practice. They also show that delayed targets can yield accurate solutions comparable in quality to those obtained with large-sample integral estimates.
icml-2024-learning-from-integral-losses-.tldr: Unbiased integral estimates can bias physics-informed training losses, and a delayed target method can recover accurate solutions.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a new task, but performance can deteriorate on distributions different from the fine-tuning data. Some methods try to prevent this by preserving the model’s pretrained representations. This paper argues that those representations can also have weaknesses, especially when the downstream task comes from a different domain or subdomain.

LEVI combines the pretrained model with a small model specialized for the new task. It adaptively ensembles them at individual layers, bringing together two different views of the task while preserving efficiency. The motivation is that neither the pretrained features nor the fine-tuning data should be treated as an entirely reliable source of useful representations.

The authors report that combining these complementary models suppresses problematic features from both sources while retaining useful task information. Broad experiments with language and vision models show substantial improvements in fine-tuning generalization. The findings support balancing inherited knowledge with task-specific learning, particularly when preserving pretrained representations too strongly could obstruct learning features that the new task needs.
icml-2024-levi-generalizable-fine-tuning.tldr: LEVI adaptively combines pretrained and task-specific models layer by layer to improve generalization after fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Predicting the composition of a bacterial community requires accounting for interactions among its members. This paper models those communities directly from bacterial genomes using graph neural networks. The structure reflects that a community is a set: changing the order in which bacteria are listed should not change the prediction about the community.

The model predicts the relative abundance of community members at steady state. By targeting this final profile directly, it learns the effects of community dynamics implicitly and avoids needing growth curves. The set-based design also supports combinatorial generalization, meaning the model can address community compositions beyond the particular combinations encountered during training.

On two real-world datasets, the authors demonstrate generalization to unseen bacteria and different community structures, which they describe as a first. They also create a simulation that allows flexible data generation and examines the effects of interaction strength, community size, and training-data quantity. The combined work connects a practical genome-based prediction method with a way to investigate how community conditions affect its predictions.
icml-2024-modelling-microbial-communitie.tldr: A genome-based graph neural network predicts steady-state bacterial abundances and generalizes to unseen bacteria and community structures in two datasets.

paragraphs: Neural networks used directly as partial differential equation solvers often have limited accuracy. This paper gives them a different role: learning preconditioners that help an iterative numerical solver work efficiently. The resulting FCG-NO method pairs neural operators with flexible conjugate gradients, combining learned assistance with an established equation-solving procedure.

The neural operators are designed to work across discretizations, so their use is not tied to a single resolution. Architecture, loss function, and training-data collection are developed together to learn effective preconditioners. Flexible conjugate gradient theory permits nonlinear preconditioners in this setting, and the learned preconditioners can be applied in O(N) operations without imposing a restricted preconditioner-matrix form.

Ablation studies investigate the contributions of the loss and training-data collection scheme. Numerical results compare favorably with classical preconditioners and demonstrate reuse of preconditioners trained at lower resolution on higher-resolution data. The findings support using neural operators to accelerate numerical solving while addressing the accuracy problem that motivates moving away from standalone learned solvers.
icml-2024-neural-operators-meet-conjugat.tldr: FCG-NO learns neural-operator preconditioners for flexible conjugate gradients, with favorable numerical results and transfer across resolutions.

paragraphs: Strategic classification considers people who alter their inputs in response to a decision rule. Learning a robust classifier therefore requires accounting for how people may react. This paper studies the case where those reactions are uncertain and the classifier must be deployed only once, making repeated deployment an unavailable way to learn about responses.

The uncertainty centers on the costs people face when changing their inputs. For a broad class of costs, the authors prove that even a small estimation error can produce trivial accuracy in the worst case. They respond by formulating a minimax objective: choose the classifier that minimizes the largest risk across a specified set of possible costs.

The paper provides efficient full-batch and stochastic algorithms that converge offline to the minimax solution at a rate of roughly T⁻¹ᐟ², up to logarithmic factors. Its analysis also identifies the value of dual norm regularization tied to the cost function. The guarantee concerns robustness over the chosen uncertainty set, addressing the need to commit without experimenting through multiple deployments.
icml-2024-one-shot-strategic-classificat.tldr: The paper develops minimax algorithms for deploying a single classifier when people’s strategic response costs are uncertain.

paragraphs: Many scientific and machine-learning problems depend on finding the leading eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a linear operator. In high-dimensional settings, neural networks offer a way to represent these functions as an alternative to classical numerical linear algebra. This paper develops an optimization framework for learning the leading singular values and singular functions of an operator.

The framework starts from the characterization of a truncated singular value decomposition as a low-rank approximation. It adds techniques called nesting to learn the top L components in the correct order. Ordering matters because the goal is to identify the leading components, not merely obtain a collection of functions that provides an approximation.

The method implicitly encourages the desired orthogonality between learned functions through an unconstrained objective. This avoids making explicit orthogonality constraints part of the optimization problem and permits standard gradient-based optimizers. Demonstrations in computational physics and machine learning show the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution brings ordered component learning and efficient orthogonality promotion into a single neural-network optimization formulation.
icml-2024-operator-svd-with-neural-netwo.tldr: Nested low-rank approximation trains neural networks to learn ordered leading operator singular functions while implicitly promoting orthogonality.

paragraphs: The Rashomon Effect describes situations in which many different models predict equally well on the same dataset. This position paper argues that this multiplicity can be useful, especially for noisy tabular problems. When several models perform similarly, selecting a model becomes an opportunity to consider qualities beyond predictive performance alone.

The authors discuss how this flexibility relates to finding simple but accurate models and accommodating preferences such as fairness or monotonicity without sacrificing performance. They also examine uncertainty across predictions, fairness assessments, and explanations, along with the reliability of variable importance. The existence of several good models therefore affects both which model is chosen and how its behavior should be interpreted.

The paper further connects the phenomenon to algorithm selection and public policy, and discusses a theory of when and why it arises. Its position is conditional on the availability of many equally good models, a phenomenon reported for many real datasets. The proposed shift is to treat that collection as a resource for addressing practical and societal requirements.
icml-2024-position-amazing-things-come-f.tldr: When many models predict equally well, their diversity can offer flexibility in simplicity, fairness, explanations, and practical decision-making.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that machine learning undervalues research driven by concrete applications. Its central point is that a real-world challenge can inspire algorithmic innovation with significance beyond the original application. As machine learning spreads into more domains, the authors regard this source of new ideas as increasingly important to the field itself.

The paper describes application-driven research and compares it with the more conventional practice of starting from a method. It emphasizes that the two approaches can strengthen one another. Under this view, solving an application problem can contribute to machine-learning methodology, while methods research can supply ideas that help address the application’s demands.

The authors also identify reviewing, hiring, and teaching practices as obstacles to application-driven innovation and outline improvements to those processes. The contribution is an argument about research priorities and institutional evaluation, supported by an account of the approach’s benefits. It asks the community to recognize potential methodological contributions arising from applications, rather than judging their value only within the application domain.
icml-2024-position-application-driven-in.tldr: The authors argue that application-driven research can advance machine learning itself and deserves stronger support in evaluation, hiring, and teaching.

paragraphs: Discussions of large language models often make broad claims about what these systems are and what they can do. This position paper argues that the discussion lacks a shared working definition and depends on assumptions that deserve closer examination. Its starting point is conceptual clarity: claims about a category of models are harder to assess when that category is not clearly defined.

The authors contribute a definition of large language models and critically examine five common claims about their properties. These include claims concerning emergent properties. The aim is to revisit the reasoning and assumptions behind familiar statements, making the framing of research claims itself an object of analysis.

The paper concludes with suggestions for future research and for how that research should be presented. Its contribution is therefore a proposed definition, a critical examination of common claims, and a discussion of research direction. The central implication is that productive debate about language-model capabilities requires attention to both the meaning of the terms used and the qualifications attached to claims.
icml-2024-position-key-claims-in-llm-res.tldr: This position paper proposes an LLM definition and reexamines five common claims, including claims about emergent properties.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that satellite data should be recognized as a distinct machine-learning modality. The authors contend that practices developed for traditional data types can be poorly suited to satellite data. Their proposed response is a research agenda organized around its particular characteristics and challenges, with the goal of improving both research quality and real-world impact.

The argument extends across theory, methods, and deployment. Recognizing a separate modality would make satellite data a central consideration in how research problems are framed, rather than treating it only as a setting in which existing methods are applied. The authors present this as an opportunity to rethink machine-learning practices as work on satellite data gains traction.

The paper offers research directions, discussion questions, and actionable suggestions for developing satellite machine learning into a dedicated discipline. Its stated ambition is to contribute to substantial challenges for both machine learning and society. This is a proposed disciplinary shift: the paper makes a case for what the research community should prioritize and how that agenda could increase the field’s impact.
icml-2024-position-mission-critical-sate.tldr: The authors argue for treating satellite data as a distinct modality with its own machine-learning research agenda.

paragraphs: Predictive coding is a biologically plausible learning approach studied as an alternative to conventional deep-learning methods. Such alternatives are of interest for fast, low-energy neuromorphic implementations, where backpropagation presents limitations. This paper investigates whether predictive coding can support causal inference, extending its capabilities beyond learning correlations in observed data.

The authors show that a simple modification to predictive coding’s inference process enables computation of interventions. The procedure does not require deleting parts of a causal graph or redefining that graph. They then explore settings in which the graph is unknown and must be inferred from observational data, bringing causal-structure learning into the investigation.

Experiments show that these findings can improve predictive coding’s performance on image-classification tasks. The authors interpret the results as evidence that predictive coding models can perform causal inference through a biologically plausible form of message passing. The work thus links an inference mechanism to both causal tasks and an observed classification benefit; its neuromorphic motivation is distinct from the empirical classification result.
icml-2024-predictive-coding-beyond-corre.tldr: A change to predictive coding’s inference process enables causal interventions and supports empirical improvements in image classification.

paragraphs: AudioSeal addresses audio authenticity by watermarking AI-generated speech so that the watermark can be detected locally. The goal includes identifying where marked speech occurs, with detection reaching the level of individual audio samples. This makes localization a central part of the method, alongside the broader task of recognizing watermarked audio.

The system jointly trains a watermark generator and detector using a localization loss. It also introduces a perceptual loss inspired by auditory masking to make the watermark harder to hear. These training objectives address complementary requirements: the signal should remain detectable by the system while being unobtrusive to a listener.

Automatic and human evaluations report leading performance for both imperceptibility and robustness to real-world audio manipulations. A single-pass detector also achieves detection speeds up to two orders of magnitude faster than existing models. These results support the method’s suitability for large-scale and real-time uses. Its proactive approach relies on embedding and recognizing a watermark, with localization providing information about the marked portions of speech.
icml-2024-proactive-detection-of-voice-c.tldr: AudioSeal combines localized speech watermarking with robust, imperceptible signals and a fast single-pass detector.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a model to guide the choice of points at which to evaluate a function. This paper considers Gaussian process models and asks how effectively exploration can be performed by drawing random samples from a distribution. The appeal is computational: selecting queries this way avoids repeatedly optimizing a potentially expensive nonconvex acquisition function.

The authors establish optimal error rates for random exploration using new concentration bounds in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. They then develop an algorithm that combines random exploration with shrinking the search domain. For this algorithm, they prove order-optimal regret guarantees in both noisy and noise-free settings, providing a theoretical basis for its query-selection strategy.

In the noise-free case, the analysis closes an existing regret gap under a mild assumption on the underlying function, partially resolving a COLT open problem. That qualification matters: the claimed resolution is partial and conditional. Together, the results show that random query selection can offer computational advantages while retaining strong regret guarantees in the studied setting.
icml-2024-random-exploration-in-bayesian.tldr: Random exploration with domain shrinking achieves order-optimal Bayesian-optimization regret while avoiding expensive acquisition-function optimization.

paragraphs: Diffusion models applied to sequences commonly use the same noise level for successive frames. Rolling Diffusion changes that arrangement to reflect the greater uncertainty associated with the more distant future. Instead of treating every frame equally during diffusion, it assigns more noise to frames appearing later in the sequence.

The method uses a sliding window for denoising. Within this temporal setup, corruption increases toward later frames as generation unfolds. The central idea is to make the noise pattern follow time, so the process distinguishes nearer frames from more uncertain future ones. This introduces temporal structure into how diffusion handles a sequence, beyond simply applying a common noise level across its frames.

The authors report empirical advantages over standard diffusion when temporal dynamics are complex. They demonstrate this in video prediction on Kinetics-600 and in forecasting chaotic fluid dynamics. These findings support the proposed treatment of future uncertainty in the tested settings, with the strongest stated conclusion tied to complex dynamics rather than every possible temporal-generation task.
icml-2024-rolling-diffusion-models-1d1b6.tldr: Rolling Diffusion gives later frames more noise and uses sliding-window denoising, improving prediction in tested settings with complex temporal dynamics.

paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty through probabilities over possible labels. A second-order prediction goes further by placing a distribution over those probability distributions. This richer representation has motivated methods for separating and measuring types of predictive uncertainty, but recent criticism has identified undesirable theoretical behavior in some commonly used measures.

The paper responds by proposing formal criteria for what a meaningful uncertainty measure based on second-order distributions should satisfy. This makes the desired behavior of the measure explicit before choosing a particular formula. The authors then introduce a general framework for constructing measures with those requirements in mind, linking the definition of uncertainty to mathematical properties.

They instantiate the framework using Wasserstein distance and prove that the resulting measures satisfy all the proposed criteria. The contribution is therefore both a set of standards and a construction meeting them. The guarantee is specifically about those formal criteria, providing a principled answer to the theoretical concerns motivating the work without establishing that every question about predictive uncertainty has been settled.
icml-2024-second-order-uncertainty-quant.tldr: The paper defines criteria for second-order uncertainty measures and proves that a Wasserstein-based construction satisfies them.

paragraphs: Classifier-free guidance is a technique for encouraging generated outputs to follow a prompt. This paper demonstrates its use during inference in language models, investigating whether guidance can improve both task performance and adherence to user instructions. The study covers Pythia, GPT-2, and models in the LLaMA family across a broad collection of benchmarks.

Reported improvements span question answering, reasoning, code generation, and translation. On LAMBADA, the authors report a state-of-the-art result with LLaMA-7B exceeding PaLM-540B. They also describe gains equivalent to those of a model with twice as many parameters. These comparisons concern the reported evaluations, showing that generation-time guidance can provide substantial benefits without making parameter count the only route to improvement.

Guidance can also be combined with Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, producing additional gains on difficult tasks. For challenging prompts specifying form or content, the authors report improved faithfulness and coherence, with human evaluators preferring guided outputs 75% of the time. The findings connect benchmark gains with better adherence in assistant-style generation.
icml-2024-stay-on-topic-with-classifier-.tldr: Classifier-free guidance improves language-model task performance and prompt adherence, with guided outputs preferred in 75% of the reported human evaluations.

paragraphs: Language models typically generate tokens sequentially, which limits inference speed. Tandem Transformers combine a small autoregressive model with a large model that processes blocks of tokens together. The small model can attend to the large model’s representations, using that richer information to improve its predictions while retaining its role in sequential generation.

On the PaLM2 pretraining dataset, pairing PaLM2-Bison with PaLM2-Gecko improves next-token prediction accuracy by 3.3% over Gecko alone. The tandem also runs 1.16 times as fast as PaLM2-Otter while achieving comparable downstream performance. These comparisons show how sharing representations can improve the small model and yield a useful speed-performance tradeoff for the evaluated models.

The authors additionally integrate the tandem into the SPEED speculative-decoding framework, where the large model validates the small model’s proposed tokens. In that setting, the Bison-Gecko tandem is around 1.14 times as fast as using ordinary Gecko within SPEED, while maintaining identical downstream task accuracy. The two evaluations illustrate distinct uses of the same collaboration between a smaller generator and a larger model.
icml-2024-tandem-transformers-for-infere.tldr: Tandem Transformers let a small generator use a larger model’s representations, improving prediction accuracy and inference speed in reported PaLM2 evaluations.
